Bright Data is the better choice for hard targets and large pipelines, where its much bigger pool, carrier targeting, Web Unlocker and SERP API pay for themselves, and its rates fall to $2.50/GB. Bright Data and Infatica both emphasise compliance and ethical sourcing, which puts them on the shortlist of procurement-conscious buyers. Infatica is a mid-market network with 35M-40M IPs, ZIP targeting on every plan, a $4 seven-day trial and a rare IPv6 residential pool. blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data is the largest and most complete web-data platform in this market. Beyond residential proxies it sells datacenter, ISP and mobile networks, an unblocking API, a SERP API, a hosted Scraping Browser and ready-made datasets, each billed on its own meter. Its residential network is advertised at more than 150 million IPs in 195 countries, with targeting down to ZIP code and ASN. The trade-off is cost and complexity: the list price sits at the top of the market and the dashboard is built around zones, rules and compliance checks rather than a two-click setup.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica is a web-data provider with offices in the UK, Singapore and the UAE. It started with premium residential proxies and now sells mobile, static ISP, datacenter and IPv6 residential networks plus scraper APIs and datasets. Its residential pool is advertised at 35M-40M IPs in 195 countries, with ZIP-level targeting on every plan, and the company is unusually explicit about sourcing: it says it does not resell IPs and lists several ISO certifications.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Infatica

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

For a 10 GB month, Infatica costs about $40 while Bright Data costs about $80, so Infatica saves around 50%. For a 100 GB month, Infatica costs about $360 while Bright Data costs about $499, so Infatica saves around 28%. Both Bright Data and Infatica work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Bright Data (150M+) is about 4.3x larger than Infatica (35M-40M). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. How Infatica compares: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How Infatica compares: ZIP targeting helps local search results.

Social media and multi-account management: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Bright Data: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work. Infatica: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature. Let price and the countries you need decide.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. The limitation on the Infatica side: ZIP-level targeting for local prices.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How Infatica compares: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing.

Tight budgets: Infatica wins. The deciding factor for Infatica: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes. The limitation on the Bright Data side: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Infatica before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs Infatica faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, Infatica in 1, and 1 is a tie. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
